paragraphs.title: The Censers of the Sinners as a Covering for the Altar

easy.question: Who was commanded to take up the censers from among the burning?
answers: Moses
Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest
Aaron
easy.explanation: In Numbers 16:37 (KJV), it is written: "Speak unto Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest, that he take up the censers".

easy.question: What did they eventually turn the censers into?
answers: Musical instruments
A decoration for the Tabernacle
A covering for the altar
easy.explanation: In Numbers 16:38-39 (KJV), it is described that the censers were beaten into "broad plates for a covering of the altar".

easy.question: Why were the censers considered holy, even though they belonged to sinners?
answers: Because Moses touched them
Because they were offered before the Lord
Because they were made of pure gold
easy.explanation: In Numbers 16:38 (KJV), it is stated: "for they offered them before the Lord, therefore they are hallowed".

medium.question: What was the primary purpose of turning the censers into a covering for the altar?
answers: To serve as a sign and memorial to the children of Israel
To improve the appearance of the altar
To punish Eleazar for his actions
medium.explanation: In Numbers 16:38 and 16:40 (KJV), it is said that the censers will be "a sign unto the children of Israel" and "a memorial to the children of Israel".

medium.question: In Numbers 16:39 (KJV), the censers were to be made into 'broad plates'. What does this imply about their form?
answers: They were large containers
They were flattened and hammered sheets
They were ornate sculptures
medium.explanation: The Hebrew word 'rikuei' (broad plates) comes from a root meaning to flatten by beating, indicating thin, hammered sheets of metal.

medium.question: What specific warning was given through the memorial of the censers?
answers: Not to complain against the Lord and Moses
Not to touch the altar without permission
Not to offer incense unless he is of the seed of Aaron
medium.explanation: In Numbers 16:40 (KJV), it is stated: "to the end that no stranger, which is not of the seed of Aaron, come near to offer incense before the Lord".

challenge.question: The verse refers to people who died in 'the fire' and the censers of 'these sinners against their own souls'. Which group does it implicitly mention through this reference?
answers: The company of Korah who rebelled against Moses and Aaron
The group of Israelites who complained in the wilderness
The people who did not believe in the ability to conquer the land
challenge.explanation: In Numbers 16:40 (KJV), it is explicitly stated that the purpose is "that he be not as Korah, and as his company," which implies that "those who were burned" and "the sinners" in the preceding verses refer to Korah and his rebellious company.

challenge.question: The verse states that the censers 'became holy' even though they belonged to sinners. What is the theological significance of this consecration?
answers: That God forgave the sinners for their actions
That an object designated or offered to the Lord acquires an independent holiness that does not depend on the purity of the offerer
That the holiness of the object disappeared with the death of the sinners
challenge.explanation: The fact that the censers became holy ("for they offered them before the Lord, therefore they are hallowed") even though they belonged to sinners ("these censers of the sinners against their own souls") emphasizes that once an object is designated or offered to the Lord, it acquires a sacred status, requiring special treatment, regardless of the merit of the offerer.

challenge.question: Why is it important to mention that Eleazar the priest is the son of Aaron (Numbers 16:37 KJV)?
answers: To highlight his special role as the senior priest
To note that he was the only priest who survived the plague
To clarify that he is the legitimate successor of Aaron and authorized to handle holy objects
challenge.explanation: The mention of the lineage "son of Aaron the priest" emphasizes Eleazar's legitimacy to handle holy objects, especially in the context of Korah's rebellion, which challenged the legitimacy of the priesthood, and prepares the ground for the explanation in Numbers 16:40 (KJV) about the prohibition of offering incense by a stranger who is not of Aaron's seed.

paragraphs.title: The Complaints of the Children of Israel and the Plague

easy.question: Against whom did the children of Israel complain in this chapter?
answers: Against Korah and his company
Against Moses and Aaron
Against God
easy.explanation: Numbers 16:41 (KJV) explicitly states: "And all the congregation of the children of Israel murmured on the morrow against Moses and against Aaron".

easy.question: What did the Lord tell Moses and Aaron to do so they would not be destroyed with the congregation?
answers: To bring sacrifices
To separate from the midst of the congregation
To pray within the congregation
easy.explanation: In Numbers 16:45 (KJV), the Lord tells them: "Get you up from among this congregation, that I may consume them as in a moment".

easy.question: What did Aaron take to make atonement for the people and stop the plague?
answers: A staff
A stone
A censer with fire and incense
easy.explanation: Numbers 16:46 (KJV) describes Moses' instruction to Aaron: "Take a censer, and put fire therein from off the altar, and put on incense".

medium.question: Why did Moses order Aaron to hasten to the congregation with the incense?
answers: Because the children of Israel were rushing to depart.
Because wrath had already gone out and the plague had begun.
Because it was time to offer the daily sacrifice.
medium.explanation: Numbers 16:46 (KJV) explains the urgency: "for there is wrath gone out from the Lord; the plague is begun." The plague had already begun, therefore it was necessary to act quickly.

medium.question: In Numbers 16:41 (KJV), it states that 'all the congregation of the children of Israel murmured'. What does 'murmured' mean in this context?
answers: They rejoiced
They complained quietly
They bowed down in worship
medium.explanation: To 'murmur' means to complain or express dissatisfaction, often in a low, indistinct tone. The verse describes the Israelites' complaints against Moses and Aaron.

medium.question: How many people died in the plague described in these verses?
answers: 14,700 in addition to those who died because of Korah
14,700 including those who died because of Korah
Only those who died because of Korah, without a specified number
medium.explanation: Numbers 16:49 (KJV) specifies: "Now they that died in the plague were fourteen thousand and seven hundred, beside them that died about the matter of Korah," meaning this number is in addition to the previous deaths.

challenge.question: What is the significance of Moses and Aaron 'falling on their faces' (Numbers 16:45 KJV) after hearing the word of the Lord?
answers: They fainted from fear and panic.
They fell on their faces as a gesture of prayer, intercession, and humility before the Lord.
They hid from the Lord so they would not be destroyed with the congregation.
challenge.explanation: Falling on one's face in the Bible is a posture of humility, supplication, and intercession before the Lord, especially in times of crisis and danger, as they intercede on behalf of the people.

challenge.question: What is the connection between the 'glory of the Lord' that appeared (Numbers 16:42 KJV) and the beginning of the plague?
answers: The glory of the Lord appeared as a message of peace and blessing to the people.
The appearance of the glory of the Lord signified God's immediate intervention in the people's complaint, which led to wrath and plague.
The glory of the Lord appeared only to frighten Moses and Aaron.
challenge.explanation: The appearance of the glory of the Lord is often accompanied by a revelation of divine anger or judgment, and in this case, it precedes the Lord's words to Moses and Aaron to separate from the congregation before He would destroy them in a plague, as a result of His anger at their complaint.

challenge.question: Why did Aaron stand 'between the dead and the living' (Numbers 16:48 KJV) with the incense?
answers: To ensure that all the dead were properly buried.
To draw a physical boundary line separating the living from the dead.
To symbolize his role as an intercessor and atoner, through whom the plague is stopped and the barrier of death is halted.
challenge.explanation: Aaron's standing between the dead and the living, with the atoning incense in his hand, is a powerful symbolic act. It expresses his unique role as the priest representing the people before the Lord and stopping the severe decree, placing him as a barrier against the spreading death.

easy.question: How many rods did the Lord command Moses to gather from the children of Israel?
answers: Twelve rods
Ten rods
Eight rods
easy.explanation: In Numbers 17:2 (KJV), it is explicitly stated: "take of every one of them a rod according to the house of their fathers... twelve rods".

easy.question: Where did Moses lay the rods after he gathered them?
answers: Outside the camp
Inside the tabernacle of the congregation before the testimony
On the mountain
easy.explanation: In Numbers 17:4 (KJV), it is said: "And thou shalt lay them up in the tabernacle of the congregation before the testimony".

easy.question: Which rod budded and brought forth buds, bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds?
answers: The rod of the prince of the tribe of Judah
The rod of Moses
The rod of Aaron for the house of Levi
easy.explanation: In Numbers 17:8 (KJV), it is explicitly described: "And, behold, the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds".

medium.question: What was the primary purpose of the test with the rods, as stated in Numbers 17:5 (KJV)?
answers: To choose the next king for the children of Israel
To quiet the complaints of the children of Israel and show God's choice
To ensure that each tribe had its own rod
medium.explanation: In Numbers 17:5 (KJV), it is explicitly stated: "and I will make to cease from me the murmurings of the children of Israel, whereby they murmur against you," meaning the purpose was to stop the complaints by proving God's choice.

medium.question: In Numbers 17:5 (KJV), God says 'I will make to cease from me the murmurings of the children of Israel'. What does 'murmurings' refer to?
answers: Their blessings
Their praises
Their complaints or grumbling
medium.explanation: The term 'murmurings' refers to expressions of discontent, complaints, or grumbling from the people against God and their leaders.

medium.question: After Aaron's rod blossomed, what did the Lord command Moses to do with the rod?
answers: To return it to Levi
To keep it before the Testimony as a memorial and a sign
To burn it
medium.explanation: In Numbers 17:10 (KJV), the Lord commanded Moses: "Bring Aaron's rod again before the testimony, to be kept for a token against the rebels".

challenge.question: In Numbers 17:8 (KJV), it is described that Aaron's rod 'brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds'. What is the special significance of a dry rod yielding almonds, beyond general blossoming?
answers: The almonds symbolize food for the people
The almond is the tree that blossoms faster than all other trees and symbolizes the speed and certainty of divine choice
The almonds are unripe fruit, indicating the beginning of the blossoming process
challenge.explanation: The almond is known as the tree that blossoms first in spring (hence its Hebrew name - shaked, for its haste), and the yielding of ripe almonds from a dry rod emphasizes not only a miracle of blossoming but also the speed, certainty, and completeness of God's choice of Aaron.

challenge.question: Why was 'Aaron's name' (Numbers 17:3 KJV) written on Aaron's rod, representing the tribe of Levi, and not 'Levi' like the other rods on which the names of the tribal princes were written?
answers: To distinguish Aaron from the rest of the sons of Levi who had already been chosen to serve
To emphasize Aaron's unique status as high priest, personally chosen, beyond representing his tribe
Because Aaron did not have his own tribe but was counted among the tribe of Levi
challenge.explanation: While the other rods represented their tribes through their princes, the specific inscription of Aaron's name emphasizes his personal selection for the role of high priesthood, whose status and function were unique and distinct from the roles of the other sons of Levi.

challenge.question: In Numbers 17:10 (KJV), it is said that Aaron's rod should be brought back 'to be kept for a token against the rebels; and thou shalt quite take away their murmurings from me, that they die not'. What deep meaning do the words 'that they die not' carry in this context?
answers: That they should not abandon the way of the Lord and continue to rebel against Him
That they should not physically die as a result of a plague for their continued complaints
That they should not move the rod from its place
challenge.explanation: The words 'that they die not' in the context of 'against the rebels' and 'that their murmurings may cease' refer to the danger of death as a divine punishment for rebellions and complaints, as occurred in previous instances. The purpose of the sign is to prevent them from continuing their rebellion, thereby preventing the terrible punishment of death.

paragraphs.title: The People's Fear of the Tabernacle

easy.question: Who speaks to Moses in these verses?
answers: The children of Israel
Aaron
Levites
easy.explanation: Numbers 17:12 (KJV) begins with: "And the children of Israel spake unto Moses".

easy.question: What main feeling is expressed in the words of the children of Israel to Moses in Numbers 17:12 (KJV)?
answers: Joy and gratitude
Fear and despair
Anger and frustration
easy.explanation: The words 'Behold, we die, we perish, we all perish' express deep fear and a sense of loss and annihilation.

easy.question: What will happen to anyone who 'cometh any thing near unto the tabernacle of the Lord', according to the words of the children of Israel in Numbers 17:13 (KJV)?
answers: Will receive a reward
Will be blessed
Will die
easy.explanation: Numbers 17:13 (KJV) explicitly says: "Whosoever cometh any thing near... unto the tabernacle of the Lord shall die".

medium.question: What is the main reason for the fear of the children of Israel, as conveyed by their words in these verses?
answers: Lack of food in the wilderness
The fear that anyone who approaches the tabernacle of the Lord will die
An impending war with neighboring nations
medium.explanation: The children of Israel express great fear of approaching the Tabernacle by saying, in Numbers 17:13 (KJV), 'Whosoever cometh any thing near unto the tabernacle of the Lord shall die'.

medium.question: What conclusion did the children of Israel reach regarding their situation, as implied by the question 'shall we be consumed with dying' (Numbers 17:13 KJV)?
answers: They believe they are about to successfully complete their journey in the wilderness.
They wonder if the time has come when everyone will die and perish.
They are sure that only individuals will manage to survive.
medium.explanation: The rhetorical question 'shall we be consumed with dying' reflects deep despair and a feeling that they are all about to die.

medium.question: In Numbers 17:13 (KJV), the people ask, 'shall we be consumed with dying?' What does 'consumed with dying' mean?
answers: Will we rejoice in death?
Will we be completely destroyed by death?
Will we approach death?
medium.explanation: The phrase 'consumed with dying' expresses a profound sense of despair and the fear of being utterly annihilated by death.

challenge.question: In Numbers 17:13 (KJV), the people say, 'Whosoever cometh any thing near unto the tabernacle of the Lord shall die'. What does the phrase 'any thing near' emphasize?
answers: The importance of seeking proximity to God.
The certainty that even the slightest unauthorized approach will result in death.
The different types of people allowed to approach.
challenge.explanation: The phrase 'any thing near' emphasizes the absolute certainty that even the slightest unauthorized approach to the Tabernacle, regardless of intent, would result in death.

challenge.question: How do the words of the children of Israel in Numbers 17:12 (KJV) ('Behold, we die, we perish, we all perish...') reflect their overall mental state in light of the recent preceding events in previous chapters (Korah's rebellion and the plague)?
answers: They express a feeling of renewed hope after miracles.
They reflect only fatigue and impatience.
They express deep despair and a continuous sense of annihilation, as if a decree of death pursues them.
challenge.explanation: After events like Korah's rebellion and the plague (Numbers 16-17), in which thousands of people died, the children of Israel feel that they are under a constant threat of death and annihilation. The expression 'Behold, we die, we perish' expresses chronic despair.

challenge.question: Based on the words of the children of Israel in Numbers 17:13 (KJV), what can be inferred about their perception of the relationship between human beings and the Tabernacle of the Lord at that time?
answers: They see the Tabernacle as an accessible and safe place for all Israel.
They see the Tabernacle as a holy and dangerous place, from which one must keep away to prevent death.
They see the Tabernacle as a place intended only for general prayer.
challenge.explanation: The children of Israel say 'Whosoever cometh any thing near... unto the tabernacle of the Lord shall die,' which indicates their perception of the Tabernacle as a dangerous and threatening place, where proximity to it brings the punishment of death, and not as an accessible or safe place.
